problems.title: The threshold-crossing index is not the component count
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, PDF p.6; current FusionBench fusion_bench/method/dop/dop.py, SVD searchsorted and subspace slices
claim: `dop.py` uses the zero-based crossing index as the rank in a slice.
analysis: For singular values \((3,1)\), a \(0.9\) cumulative threshold crosses at index \(1\), but keeping one component captures only \(0.75\) of the mass. For \((1,0)\), crossing index zero yields an empty subspace, zero proxy and potentially undefined zero-loss normalization.
result: The public rank selection omits the crossing component.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Convert index to count by adding one, with separate rules for zero total mass and zero normalization losses.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a local rank-selection defect without measured central experimental impact.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Normalized-gradient coefficients do not give raw-gradient common descent
problems.source_location: Eq.(3), PDF pp.6–7; current FusionBench fusion_bench/method/dop/dop.py, gradient_normalizers, MinNormSolver and scaled backward
claim: Equation (3) chooses coefficients for a minimum-norm combination, but the release solves using loss-normalized gradients and applies the coefficients to raw gradients.
analysis: At \(w=1\), losses \(8w^2\) and \(32(w-2)^2\) have raw gradients \(16,-64\), normalized gradients \(2,-2\), and normalized coefficient \(1/2\). Applying that coefficient to raw gradients gives \(-24\), so subtracting the direction increases the first loss. The default smoothed coefficients approximately \((0.7997,0.2003)\) still give \(-0.024\), whereas raw minimum-norm coefficients \((0.8,0.2)\) give zero.
result: This release step lacks the stated per-step common-descent property. It does not determine every final Pareto status.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Use the same gradients for coefficient selection and application. Treat coefficient smoothing as a changed algorithm unless a separate descent check preserves the required inequalities.
problems.impact_rationale: The counterexample targets a local released update, without established damage to the central experimental result.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The raw-gradient span argument does not automatically extend to Adam
problems.source_location: Properties 4.1–4.2, pp. 5–6; Adam fine-tuning in Appendix C, p. 25.
claim: Properties 4.1–4.2 derive a task-vector span relation by scalar-step gradient-descent telescoping, while expert training includes Adam.
analysis: For input \(x=(1,2)\), zero initial weight and an appropriate squared loss, the raw gradient is \((-1,-2)\). Adam’s first normalized update is approximately \((0.1,0.1)\), outside the one-dimensional span of \(x\). Coordinatewise preconditioning need not preserve a raw-gradient span.
result: The scalar-gradient-descent proposition survives with its optimizer restriction. Its extension to all Adam-trained experts is not justified.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Restrict updates to scalar linear combinations of historical raw gradients, or analyze the actual preconditioned update spaces.
problems.impact_rationale: This qualifies a supporting optimizer assumption rather than disproving the core empirical method.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: A task-vector proxy need not cover the full old input subspace
problems.source_location: Section 3.2.2, p. 5; Section 4.2 proxy-retention interpretation, p. 6.
claim: The retention interpretation treats zero projection loss in retained task-vector directions as protecting all old inputs.
analysis: Let \(W_0=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\), \(W_o=I\), and \(W_n=W^*=\operatorname{diag}(1,3)\). The old task vector is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\); both stated task proxies vanish, yet old input \(e_2\) changes output from \(e_2\) to \(3e_2\). Directions unchanged by old fine-tuning can still matter to old prediction.
result: Zero proxy is not a universal old-task preservation theorem. The paper’s approximation language remains material.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.
repair: Full preservation follows if the retained task subspace covers the old input subspace and the corresponding projection loss is zero. Mere containment in the opposite direction is insufficient.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a proxy-coverage limitation; actual old-task accuracy loss is not measured.
problems.existing_correction_status: An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.
